title: The Fox Who Read the Sand
summary: A hunter follows the pale fox down to the cliffs and learns to read the tracks that the wind leaves in the sand.
moral: The world writes down what it knows; only the patient learn to read it.
attribution: A traditional Dogon tale, retold for Ubuntu Tales.

cover.alt: A pale fox crossing patterned sand beneath a grid of stars and a dark cliff silhouette

sentences.text: The Dogon country is a country of stone and sand, where the cliffs of Bandiagara stand above the plain like a wall built before memory.
The old people say that in the earliest days the pale fox walked there alone, and that it always walked at an angle to the paths of everyone else.
A hunter was following a trail of antelope tracks one evening when he saw the first prints of the fox.
The tracks crossed and recrossed, went down into a dry gully and came up again without ever leading to a den.
The hunter followed them until the light began to fail.
At the foot of the cliff he found the fox sitting on a flat stone, watching him.
It lifted one paw, drew it through the sand in a slow curved line, and then sat back as if it had asked a question.
The hunter had never learned to read anything but the tracks of animals he wished to eat.
He knelt and looked at the line in the sand for a long time.
Then he saw that the curve was the shape of the dry gully, and the small dots beside it were the places where water had once stood.
The fox rose and walked on.
The hunter followed it for the rest of the night, and by morning he understood a little of what the old people meant: the sand keeps a record of what has passed, and the fox is only reading it aloud.
After that the hunter became one of the men who are consulted on questions, because he could look at a patch of ground and say where the herd had gone and when.
He never claimed to be wise.
He said only that he had learned to listen to the ground, and that the fox had been the first teacher.
